results.title: Preregistration | FORRT - Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training
results.content: # Preregistration A preregistration document is time-stamped and typically registered with an independent party (e.g., a repository) so that it can be publicly shared with others (possibly after an embargo period). Preregistration provides a transparent documentation of what was planned at a certain time point, and allows third parties to assess what changes may have occurred afterwards. The more detailed a preregistration is, the better third parties can assess these changes and with that the validity of the performed analyses. **Related terms:** Confirmation bias, Confirmatory analyses, Exploratory Data Analysis, HARKing, Pre-analysis plan, Questionable Research Practices or Questionable Reporting Practices (QRPs), Registered Report, Research Protocol, Transparency **Reference:** Haven and van Grootel (2019); Lewandowsky and Bishop (2016); Merten and Krypotos (2019); Navarro (2020); Nosek et al. results.title: Reproducibility in ecology and evolution: Minimum standards for data and code
results.content: Reproducibility in ecology and evolution: Minimum standards for data and code - PMC. Reproducibility in ecology and evolution: Minimum standards for data and code. Received 2023 Mar 11; Accepted 2023 Mar 16; Collection date 2023 May. _Ecology and Evolution_ published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd. This is an open access article under the terms of the License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. However, it is no longer seen as best practice to publish just a summary of the data linked to a scientific article within our fields. Rather, open data, which should include code and supporting documentation, allow independent researchers to evaluate a study's methodologies and interpretations of data (Shaw et al.,2016) and use its primary data in new investigations, including data syntheses (Whitlock et al.,2010). For all these reasons, journals and funding bodies increasingly are requiring authors to make their data and code freely accessible (Wilkinson et al.,2016). However, there is still a great deal of variation among journals and researchers in terms of whether open data sharing should be mandated or merely encouraged and, if they are shared, whether they should be held to a minimum set of standards (Hampton et al.,2013; Herold,2015; Whitlock et al.,2010). If applied consistently, these requirements will allow contributors to be acknowledged for their work through citation (e.g., via a DOI) of open data, and facilitate scientific progress. We call for a requirement, as a condition for publication, that authors provide all raw data and metadata, code, programming scripts, and bespoke software necessary for fully replicating any analyses that lead to inferences made in a published study. 1. Detailed metadata with a README file, describing relevant details about data collection, processing, analysis and presentation (e.g., Whitlock et al.,2010). When ethically and legally permitted, authors should seek to share aggregated or anonymized data openly with their manuscript and to share richer data through an appropriate controlled access repository. results.title: Research Preregistration 101 – Association for Psychological Science – APS
results.content: Preregistering a research project involves creating a permanent record of your study plans before you look at the data. If editors or reviewers ask about flexibility in your data-analysis choices or in your predictions, your preregistered research plan will put any concerns to rest. And, if you upload your materials, plans, and results to the same site as your preregistered plan, you can see the entire research process for a completed study in one place, making it easy for you to share with others. You can preregister every detail of your study, uploading all of your research scripts, coding schemes, data-collection plans, analysis code, and so on. The first time you preregister a detailed analysis plan, you will realize how many flexible decisions you could have made when choosing your analyses after seeing the data and how those decisions could have misled you about the results of your study. Once you have preregistered one study, subsequent preregistration plans for follow-up studies can be completed quickly and easily.

results.title: Data, Code and Materials Sharing Statement - jospt
results.content: Data, Code and Materials Sharing Statement. We **strongly encourage** authors to make relevant materials and data from the study available to readers: *JOSPT Open*encourage sharing of the datasets from which the conclusions of the paper are drawn, any computer code used to generate or analyze data, and any research materials that facilitate replication of the study findings. JOSPT Open **encourages** authors to (where possible) publicly share anonymized data from where the paper's results are drawn. The methods used to analyze data are as impactful as how the data are collected.1 Sharing the code and, where appropriate, the study materials improves the reproducibility of research findings.2 6JOSPT Open **strongly encourages** authors to share the statistical code used to generate the results of their submitted paper (submitted as an appendix/supplementary file to the main manuscript or uploaded to a public repository (see information in the paragraph below) and the persistent link included in the manuscript). The journals also encourage authors to share any relevant electronic study materials, licensed for public domain sharing, that were used for data collection. Authors are responsible for ensuring that sensitive data are not shared within code unless the procedures for clinical data sharing (above) are followed. ### Data, Code and Materials Sharing Statement. Authors must include a data, code and materials sharing statement in the manuscript. There are no data or study material available.***If Data/code/materials are not available for legal or ethical reasons, this information must be included in the data, code and materials sharing statement.*. Clinical trials are defined by the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) as "any research study that prospectively assigns human participants or groups of humans to one or more health-related interventions to evaluate the effects on health outcomes."4 Clinical trials must be prospectively registered in an appropriate trial registration database, and authors are encouraged to include a statistical analysis plan in their registration.3 JOSPT Open **strongly encourages** prospective registration of systematic review protocols in the PROSPERO) database. results.title: 2 Open Data and Reproducibility | Fundamentals in Data Management for Qualitative and Quantitative Arctic Research
results.content: # 2 Open Data and Reproducibility. To enable full reproducibility by the broader community; researchers, practitioners, policy makers etc, all products of the research activity need to be accessible - open data, open code, and open publications. Computational reproducibility is the ability to document data, analyses, and models sufficiently for other researchers to be able to understand and ideally re-execute the computations that led to scientific results and conclusions. To be able to evaluate the data, analyses, and models on which conclusions are drawn, computational reproducibility requires open science approaches, including straightforward steps for archiving data and code openly along with the scientific workflows describing the provenance of scientific results (e.g., Hampton et al. Open science supports a culture of sharing research outputs and data, and FAIR focuses on how to prepare the data. Sharing sensitive data can pose challenges to researchers, however sharing metadata or anonymized data contributes to discovery, supports open science principles, and helps reduce duplicate research efforts.
